en: The Ritual for Confessing Faults:
Composed by the Tripitaka Master Yijing of the Tang Dynasty.
Every half-month, on the day of the new moon, one should recall the faults committed and confess them according to the Dharma.
Whether it be intentional lying, drinking alcohol, eating at improper times, or being invited to eat incense while having unwashed hands—whether at dawn or at other times.
They drink and use water without examining it;
because they do not release living beings according to the Dharma,
they sever the lives of sentient beings.
One destroys one's own cultivated ground,
or instructs another to destroy it,
and does not utter the words of "purification through knowledge."
They consume the five types of cultivated seeds without purifying them by means of fire or other methods;
they eat from bowls and dishes that have not been washed clean;
and they eat from bronze bowls, spoons, and chopsticks without scrubbing them with ash.
All bronze vessels must be scrubbed with ash to become clean;
if they are washed with soap-beans (zǎodòu) and water, they do not achieve purity.
This also applies to water from bottles that has been kept overnight for drinking or consumption, or which has been defiled by improper contact.
Furthermore, one eats remnants from previous nights, food touched by knives, or cakes cut with blades;
one drinks at improper times unclean tea, broth, ghee, honey, or water;
and after having consumed the five types of formal meals.
Having finished setting aside his dignified demeanor,
he swallowed the remaining saliva and personally took hold of gold, silver, coins, and jewels.
Furthermore, when causing others to receive [the robe],
one does not utter the words for "knowing purity.
Whenever touching fire, one does not maintain mindfulness.
To touch fire while burning incense and the like without maintaining mindfulness;
to enter a village at an improper time without informing a bhikṣu;
and to stay overnight for more than two nights in the same room as one who has not yet received full ordination.
Reciting together with one who has not received full ordination,
as well as chanting the name of the Buddha in unison with them—
these constitute *pāyattika* offenses.
Speaking from the perspective of those who have committed the offense repeatedly, all other cases should be judged accordingly; this offense should be confessed three times.
Furthermore, one must not chew a tooth-stick every morning or after the main meal.
Or they chew tooth-sticks and the like near a stupa,
discarding them without rinsing after use;
or they spit and snot upon the pure grounds of the Saṃgha.
Or they discard lice and the like without regard for their proper place;
or they make noise while eating and drinking;
or they speak with food still in their mouths while eating.
Or they bite off half their food;
or they sit or lie on the same bedding as those who have not yet received the full precepts;
or they urinate while standing.
Or failing to wash clean after defecating or urinating;
not rinsing the mouth and spitting water when defecating or urinating;
and failing to snap one's fingers or clear one's throat when discarding nasal mucus, saliva, or tooth-sticks.
Holding food or drink vessels with soiled hands;
drinking water or rinsing the mouth with hands that have not been washed clean;
and eating honey at improper times.
One does not perform purification with drops of water;
nor does one contemplate men or women,
failing to maintain the mind properly and thereby giving rise to thoughts of desire.
Or one may touch one's own body and give rise to a mind of lustful attachment; or,
without fixing the mind on the perception of light, one may sleep with a distracted mind,
lying down beneath the light of a lamp or candle.
Even if there is an occasion for opening [the precept], if one touches fire or the like without maintaining mindfulness,
or gives rise to a disrespectful mind toward the Triple Gem, teachers, monks, parents, or elders.
Furthermore, if one gives rise to anger and resentment and fails to endure it,
or extinguishes the lamp-light without maintaining mindfulness,
all such acts constitute offenses of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
Furthermore, to speak briefly according to necessity:
if there are any other offenses, one should confess each of them as they are remembered.
All of these must be confessed by speaking once before another person.
There are those who practice the reprimanding of the mind.
What is meant by "reprimanding the mind"?
For anyone who has left the household life:
When one violates the disciplinary teachings due to a lack of heedfulness,
one must immediately reproach oneself, saying:
"This is something I ought not to have done."
"From this day forward, I shall no longer act in such a way.
If one can constantly reproach oneself in this manner,
one will naturally not fail in any of the precepts."
One should know that this is the intended meaning of Buddhism.
Furthermore, from the time one has left the household life and received the ten precepts or the full ordination (*mahāśramaṇera*),
every single matter must be reported to one's *upādhyāya* (preceptor) or *ācārya* (instructor).
There are five matters for which it is unnecessary to announce;
what are these five? They are:
defecating and urinating.
Drink pure water and chew a tooth-stick within the same boundary,
specifically within a distance of forty-nine fathoms.
One should pay homage to the Buddha and circumambulate the stupa;
all other matters must be reported to the teacher.
If one does not report them to the teacher, [it constitutes a fault].
In each case, one incurs an *duṣkṛta* offense.
Whenever the day of the *poṣadha* arrives,
one should face a *bhikṣu* who is pure and not guilty of a different offense.
According to the gravity of the offense, one should perform the appropriate gesture of respect;
kneeling with palms joined, one should recall the name of the transgression and speak as follows.
Venerable sir, please bear this in mind:
I, the bhikṣu [Name], have committed [specify the offense, such as] intentional lying or whatever other offense may apply;
I have committed numerous root *pāyattika* offenses.
Furthermore, there are numerous offenses of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*) due to various expedient means;
or, depending on the circumstances, such as not chewing tooth-sticks and so forth,
one incurs numerous fundamental offenses of wrongdoing.
And there are numerous offenses of wrongdoing (*dukṛta*) through various skillful means. For each of these offenses,
there is a corresponding offense of expiation (*pāyattika*) for disrespecting the holy teaching.
Furthermore, regarding these skillful means, there is the offense of *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing),
as well as the offense of concealment for each instance where one fails to confess to another person.
These are the offenses committed.
I now come before the Venerable One from a state of purity;
I disclose all [faults] and do not conceal them.
By having disclosed them, I obtain peace and happiness. (Recite this three times.)
He should be asked:
"Do you see your offense?
He should reply: "I do."
"I see it.
He asked again,
"Will you be able to well protect all the precepts in the future?"
He replies, "I can guard it.
The monk being addressed should say "Oṃ bhe ga" (in Sanskrit; this term is translated as "expedient means"), for by performing this act, it serves as the expedient means for liberation.
The one confessing the offense replies,
"Sādhu," which here means "well done.
This applies if one has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
However, one should first confess before others;
subsequently, one should perform the specific ritual for the offense.
This applies if one has committed a sthūlātyaya.
As for the commission of a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense,
it should be expiated according to the Dharma.
Regarding the method for making vows after each meal, it should follow the instructions of the Vinaya.
When a bhikṣu has finished eating,
if he wishes to recite the *kīnaka-gāthā*— that is,
the verses of dedication (*dakṣiṇā-gāthā*)— he may do so.
In a quiet place, whether sitting, standing,
or walking up and down,
first recite a small sutra of one or one-and-a-half pages.
Next, recite the verse:
"The meal having been finished,
may all sentient beings vow that..."
When virtuous conduct is full, one accomplishes the ten powers.
Those who practice giving will certainly obtain its benefit and profit.
If one gives for the sake of happiness,
one will certainly obtain peace and joy in the future.
[This applies to those who provide] monasteries and dwellings.
To the assembly of monks,
the founder of the monastery,
and the celestial deities who protect the monastery.
The sovereign and his hundred officials,
teachers, monks, parents, kinsmen, and all sentient beings.
If there are those who have passed away before,
may they be reborn in the Western Land to behold Amitābha Buddha,
or be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven to behold the Venerable Maitreya.
Having cast off the dust of worldly toil, they have awakened to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
As for those currently living among us,
may they be free from illness, enjoy long life, and be adorned with merit and wisdom.
May I myself be free from all obstacles and afflictions;
may I always maintain pure precepts and not transgress the *śīla*,
feeling great dread even toward minor offenses.
They shall fully confess all committed offenses;
until the end of the future, they shall never lose their faith and shall encounter spiritual friends.
May I be born in a central land, free from the eight difficulties;
may I always maintain right view until the attainment of liberation;
and may I forever act as an uninvited friend to all sentient beings.
One should immediately dedicate this merit universally to all beings,
so that they may together emerge from the flow of existence and realize the unsurpassed fruit.
If one does not perform such recitation and make such aspirations every day, [the benefit will not be attained].
Such indolent persons do not deserve the offerings of the faithful nor the purification rites.
Their latrines and urinals must necessarily be located in a separate place.
Each door leaf shall be secured with a horizontal bolt.
This is the general rule for entering a small practice chamber or using the toilet.
Hold the vessel with both hands and do not have water in your mouth while using it for purification.
After clearing your throat or snapping your fingers two or three times, you may then proceed forward.
Once you have entered, close the door panels behind you.
Take two lumps of earth or a pinch of ash;
use half to wash the body and half to wash the left hand.
Using a tube, a trough, a cloth, or a brush are all contrary to the original ritual protocol.
Once one has emerged from outside the latrine,
the vessel may be placed upon a wooden tripod and water poured toward the body;
alternatively, it may be set upon the spleen-point so that the water flows out obliquely.
If there is no jar, it is permissible to use a basin filled with water as a substitute.
Place fifteen lumps of earth on the ground to the right, or upon bricks or wooden boards.
Seven pieces are used to wash the left hand alone;
seven pieces are used to wash both hands together;
one remains.
When about to wash the ritual vessels,
one must first thoroughly clean the brick or wooden board;
only then should the contact vessel be placed upon it.
One should take water from a pure vessel and rinse the mouth three times;
only then does one accord with the rules of purity and become fit to receive or offer salutations.
One should reverently pay homage to the Triple Gem, sit upon the various couches and mats, and recite the honored scriptures.
If one does not act in accordance with the Vinaya in this manner,
whatever one does will result in the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
Whether on a journey or while traveling by boat,
one should exercise discretion according to the circumstances.
I hope that all practitioners will do so.
Know this to be the holy teaching; do not treat it lightly as if covered by ashes, lest you ultimately fall into hell.
By upholding it with reverence, you shall obtain merit.
The offense of disparaging the Dharma arises;
since this is a constant occurrence,
it must be clearly announced and made known.
The Essential Method for Confessing Offenses and Undertaking Practice.
